title: One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a one-time genetic treatment that restores function in diseased skin by correcting enough of the long-lived epidermal stem cells that continually renew it. Their descendants would retain the restored function as older surface cells are shed. The intended result is sustained benefit in treated tissue without repeated corrective treatment. Durable local restoration already has clinical precedent; the broader capability would make that outcome reliable across different disease genes and more difficult tissue settings.

Genetic correction can take different forms. Integrating gene replacement adds a functional gene to stem cells, whereas precise editing changes a disease-causing sequence or introduces corrective DNA at a targeted location. Both could satisfy this concept if they produce durable, functional stem-cell populations with acceptable safety. Ex vivo treatment corrects cells outside the body before transplanting epidermal sheets; future in vivo approaches would need to reach and correct the relevant stem cells within the patient. Precise editing is therefore a possible route, rather than a mandatory feature of every qualifying treatment.

Scope synthesis: the proposed advance extends beyond a successful graft for one epidermolysis bullosa subtype. It seeks convincing results across distinct causal genes and includes restoration at a difficult site, such as mucosa or intact but malfunctioning epidermis. Severe ichthyoses and xeroderma pigmentosum are proposed applications; the supplied clinical evidence concerns epidermolysis bullosa. The concept does not require a single vector for every mutation, and it does not include using corrected skin as a factory for systemic drugs.

significance.text: Severe epidermolysis bullosa causes persistent skin fragility, wounds and extracutaneous disease. Correcting the regenerative source of the epidermis could sustain local tissue function despite continual cell turnover, reducing dependence on repeated corrective gene delivery. The revolutionary extension would be reliable, reproducible restoration across diseases and tissue settings, building on the substantial local benefits already demonstrated by stem-cell grafting.

Benefits at mucosal or intact-skin sites remain conditional on successful delivery, stem-cell correction or engraftment, and persistence at those sites. In particular, the February 2026 review identifies inaccessible mucosa, including the esophagus and gastrointestinal tract, as a major unresolved target. Systemic delivery might eventually expand treatment reach, but the review treats delivery to internal tissues as a development requirement, not an established substitute for local grafting.

Impact synthesis: sustained function in treated skin would not by itself establish whole-body correction, elimination of extracutaneous disease, or freedom from all subsequent care. Successful treatment of two diseases would demonstrate broader applicability, not universal mutation coverage. Nor would it establish zero genomic risk. Extension to ichthyoses or xeroderma pigmentosum could be consequential, but the supplied EB-focused evidence does not establish those diseases' current treatment status or demonstrate their correction.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable correction of enough long-lived, regenerative epidermal stem cells across distinct disease genes and tissue settings. Correcting short-lived cells alone cannot establish a persistently corrected epidermis. Koller's 2023 editorial offers an insufficient number of corrected epidermal stem cells as a possible explanation for limited maintenance in some earlier recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa graft studies. That is a hypothesis about particular outcomes, rather than proof that inadequate correction of holoclones explains every graft failure.

Delivery and tissue occupation remain separate engineering barriers. Non-integrating topical B-VEC requires repeated application; integrating stem-cell grafts can provide durable local benefit but require cell preparation and transplantation. The February 2026 review describes EB genome editing as predominantly ex vivo and preclinical, and reports that genetic correction of inaccessible gastrointestinal and esophageal mucosa had not been demonstrated. Proposed extension to intact malfunctioning epidermis adds a further requirement: corrected stem cells must become established and persist in that setting. The supplied evidence does not establish a general quantitative comparison of its difficulty with open-wound grafting.

Genomic safety and consistency across causal genes also remain barriers. Editing can produce unintended changes at the intended target as well as elsewhere in the genome, while integrating vectors require assessment of insertion-related risks. The 2026 review describes variable efficacy between loci and the potential cost and time required for mutation-specific therapies. Emerging whole-gene integration approaches may broaden treatment within certain subtypes, but they do not establish one universally applicable correction method.

Remaining uncertainty: immune responses to a restored protein are a relevant question for extending treatment across genodermatoses, but the supplied texts do not establish their general frequency, severity or unresolved status across such a platform. This concern should remain an explicit subject for investigation rather than a categorical claim that restored-protein immunity prevents durable correction.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Hirsch and colleagues' 2017 LAMB3 junctional epidermolysis bullosa case as a major demonstration of extensive epidermal regeneration. Koller's June 2023 editorial describes retroviral transgenic epidermal stem-cell grafts covering approximately 80% of a child's body surface area over three surgeries, and reports effectiveness eight years after treatment. These details are retained as the editorial's account, as characterized by the supplied review; the underlying Nature report was not independently inspected in that review. The result establishes an important local regenerative capability in a particular disease setting, rather than reproducibility across multiple causal genes or tissue types.

Historical limitations in recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa graft maintenance should be read alongside later long-term benefit. The February 2026 review reports that, after a mean follow-up of 5.9 years, 70% of treated sites across seven RDEB patients showed at least 50% wound healing. This is substantial evidence of durable local benefit. It is neither evidence of complete healing at every site nor a demonstration of whole-body correction, but it prevents earlier graft limitations from being mistaken for the current limit of the entire approach.

Vyjuvek, beremagene geperpavec or B-VEC, is an approved topical HSV-1 therapy that delivers COL7A1. Koller's 2023 editorial summarizes complete wound healing as 67% with B-VEC versus 22% with placebo at six months. The February 2026 review separately reports B-VEC wound closure of 71% at three months and 67% at six months. Those time-point percentages should not be converted into a claim that an identical 67% of wounds healed by month three and continuously remained healed through month six. The supplied summaries do not provide the wound-level evidence needed for that interpretation. B-VEC requires repeated application and does not permanently correct the epidermal stem-cell compartment.

Stanford's June 23, 2025 news release reports FDA approval on April 29, 2025 of its gene-corrected RDEB graft therapy, identifies the VIITAL publication as prademagene zamikeracel, and describes results in 11 patients with 43 wound pairs. At week 24, at least 50% healing occurred in 81% of treated wounds versus 16% of control wounds; complete healing occurred in 16% versus none. The February 2026 review identifies the approved therapy as Zevaskyn. These results concern locally applied epidermal sheets for chronic wounds and do not demonstrate mucosal or whole-body correction.

The VIITAL figures above come from the retained Stanford news release, not direct inspection of the trial paper. The supplied Lancet abstract URL was not captured. Earlier notes gave exact counts of 35 of 43 treated wounds and 7 of 43 controls reaching at least half healing; those counts are consistent with the reported rounded percentages but were not directly printed in the retained texts described by the review. The percentages and denominator are therefore the supported quantitative account here, while the exact counts remain unverified in this record.

The February 2026 CRISPR review was available in full HTML and PDF according to the supplied evidence review, correcting the earlier characterization of abstract-only access. Its broad statement about the absence of a permanent treatment must be interpreted alongside documented durable local graft benefits: the remaining gap is a broadly applicable cure, not the absence of any lasting correction. It documents continuing delivery, stem-cell targeting and genomic-safety barriers. The supplied record does not establish comprehensive coverage of developments after February 2026 through November 1, 2026; the later source-retrieval date alone does not resolve that gap.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a single corrective intervention, ex vivo or in vivo, would produce at least three years of stable restored function without further corrective treatment in treated tissue for two severe genodermatoses involving different causal genes. Molecular evidence would show that corrected epidermal stem-cell clones persist and continue to supply functional tissue. At least one demonstration would include mucosa or an intact-skin disease such as a severe ichthyosis. These are proposed evaluative thresholds, not established clinical or regulatory standards.
completion_criteria.label: Single intervention restores three-year function across two genetically distinct genodermatoses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and functional evidence: results should recur in independent patients and separately prepared treatments, with transparent reporting of the treated area, causal variants, successful and failed sites, and the functional outcome relevant to each disease. Persistent corrective DNA or protein expression alone would be insufficient without sustained tissue function. Follow-up should distinguish renewed corrective treatment from other supportive care. A successful single junctional EB graft and repeatedly dosed wound therapy remain important achieved components, but would not complete this broader demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained tissue function recurs across independent patients and treatment preparations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety evidence: assessment should match the intervention and include unintended on-target and off-target changes for editing, insertion-related risks for integrating vectors, and longitudinal evidence about the behavior of corrected clones. Delivery complications and clinically relevant responses to treatment or restored protein should also be evaluated. These proposed assessments respond to documented genomic and delivery concerns; the supplied evidence does not establish a universal numerical threshold for acceptable risk.
completion_criteria.label: Intervention-specific genomic risks, clonal behavior and clinical safety are assessed

completion_criteria.text: Interpretive boundary of the proposal: three years would establish durability over that interval, not lifelong cure. Success across two causal genes and selected tissue sites would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality. Claims should remain bounded by the treated area and tissue type, the patients studied, follow-up duration and the genomic risks the measurements can detect. Whole-body benefit, extracutaneous correction and further disease applications would each require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Claims remain bounded by demonstrated durability, breadth and detectable risks

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — DER-01, Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ: both concepts involve regenerative cells and tissue engineering. DER-02 focuses on durable genetic restoration through the epidermal stem-cell compartment; that does not by itself establish restoration of a complete skin organ with all its structures and functions.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum: improved passage could enable an in vivo route for DER-02. Crossing the surface barrier would still leave stem-cell targeting, sufficient correction, persistence and genomic safety to demonstrate. DER-02 could also succeed through ex vivo grafting without solving intact-skin delivery.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-05, Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer, and DER-06, Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field: these overlap with DER-02 in durable changes to epidermal cell populations. DER-05 targets prevention of ultraviolet-driven cancer, while DER-06 targets an established mutant field. A proposed xeroderma pigmentosum application could connect DER-02 with DER-05, but correcting an inherited defect would not automatically establish cancer prevention or removal of pre-existing mutant clones.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory, and DER-07, A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march: these address immune memory or prevention of an inflammatory disease trajectory. DER-02 instead addresses inherited defects through genetically corrected epidermal stem cells. Improved local skin function would not by itself demonstrate either selective immune-memory erasure or prevention of the atopic march.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone: both depend on establishing a durable regenerative cell population, but they target different compartments. Persistent corrected epidermal stem cells do not establish that a lost melanocyte stem-cell reservoir has been rebuilt.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-09, Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated, and DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars: all three concern durable tissue improvement, but their causal targets differ. DER-02 corrects an inherited epidermal defect; DER-09 addresses ulcer regeneration after vascular and mechanical contributors are treated; DER-10 addresses established pathological scarring. EB wound-healing results cannot establish either diabetic-ulcer regeneration or scar reversal.

change_log.change: Preserved DER-02's identity while defining completion as broader, reproducible correction across disease genes and tissue settings.
change_log.reason: Durable local stem-cell graft benefits already exist; the hypothetical advance is their reliable extension.

change_log.change: Made integrating gene replacement and precise editing distinct qualifying routes.
change_log.reason: The original completion proposal permits both, whereas other wording incorrectly implied that precise editing was mandatory.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical holoclone-failure explanation with a hypothesis about particular earlier RDEB graft outcomes.
change_log.reason: Koller presents insufficient corrected stem cells as a possible explanation, not a universal causal finding.

change_log.change: Added the longer-term RDEB result of at least 50% wound healing at 70% of treated sites across seven patients after a mean 5.9 years.
change_log.reason: The later review materially qualifies the earlier account of limited graft maintenance.

change_log.change: Separated B-VEC's reported three-month and six-month outcomes and removed the inferred continuous-healing trajectory.
change_log.reason: The supplied secondary summaries report different time-point figures without establishing wound-level continuity.

change_log.change: Used VIITAL percentages with the 43-pair denominator and identified the Stanford release as the outcome source.
change_log.reason: The Lancet artifact was unavailable, and exact counts were not directly printed in the retained evidence described by the review.

change_log.change: Corrected the 2026 review's access description from abstract-only to full HTML and PDF.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies complete retained texts and substantive passages beyond the abstract.

change_log.change: Qualified blanket language about no permanent treatment and distinguished local benefit from a broadly applicable cure.
change_log.reason: An unqualified formulation would erase documented durable correction.

change_log.change: Removed universal-vector and zero-off-target-risk requirements; retained intact-skin treatment and additional diseases as proposed extensions.
change_log.reason: Those universal requirements were unsupported and unnecessary, while broader applications remain part of the concept's intended scope.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed safety evidence to include unintended on-target changes and insertion-related risks, and bounded the three-year criterion.
change_log.reason: Safety must cover both permitted correction routes, and finite follow-up cannot prove lifelong cure.

change_log.change: Added explicit reproducibility proposals, practical boundaries and distinctions from every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Completion requires interpretable breadth and repeatability, while overlapping innovations retain separate identities.

unresolved_issues: Comprehensive coverage of developments after February 2026 through November 1, 2026 is not established by the supplied freshness record.
The exact VIITAL counts of 35 of 43 treated wounds and 7 of 43 controls remain unverified in the retained texts; the underlying Lancet artifact was not captured.

The attribution and chronology of the eight-year follow-up warrant clarification: the supplied materials associate that duration with Koller's account of the child graft case while also identifying the landmark report as published in 2017. The editorial's reported duration is preserved without an invented resolution.
The supplied B-VEC summaries do not resolve wound-level continuity between the three-month and six-month outcomes.
The evidence does not establish correction of inaccessible gastrointestinal or esophageal mucosa, or the proposed intact-skin extension.
Restored-protein immunity across genodermatoses and clinical extension to severe ichthyoses or xeroderma pigmentosum are not established by these EB-focused sources.

The three-year, two-causal-gene and difficult-site thresholds are proposals; the supplied evidence does not establish a consensus threshold or the patient numbers needed to demonstrate reproducibility.
